documents.title: What is Tellann?
documents.description: Understand behavioral quality intelligence and how Tellann turns real software behavior into actionable evidence.
documents.body: What is Tellann? Understand behavioral quality intelligence and how Tellann turns real software behavior into actionable evidence. Overview What is Tellann? is part of the product model and the evidence Tellann derives from observed software behavior. It gives teams a shared way to describe what the application actually did and which evidence supports a quality conclusion. Mental model Read this topic in the sequence Connect → Observe → Demonstrate → Model → Analyze → Investigate → Act. The same event can contribute to a session, a state transition, a workflow, a graph edge, coverage, and a report without those artifacts becoming interchangeable. How to use it Choose the application and environment first, then narrow the evidence by workflow, session, time, endpoint, or event type. Use labels and metadata to make the captured behavior explainable to someone who did not run the original scenario. Interpretation Interpret the result together with its source events and collection conditions. Observed means Tellann received evidence for the behavior; it does not independently prove that the behavior is correct, secure, accessible, or complete. Limitations and responsibilities Customers remain responsible for instrumentation scope, lawful data collection, credential handling, privacy rules, and decisions made from the evidence. Tellann masks and isolates data according to configuration, but cannot infer every domain specific sensitive field. Related concepts Continue with the adjacent pages in Overview to connect this concept to its inputs, derived artifacts, and operational checks. The previous and next links follow the canonical learning order.

documents.title: Install Tellann Desktop
documents.description: Install Tellann Desktop on Windows, sign in through your browser, and connect your first project.
documents.body: Install Tellann Desktop Tellann Desktop connects projects on your computer to Tellann. It runs guided browser QA sessions, drafts expected flows from product documents, and proposes bounded SDK instrumentation that you review before any file changes. Before you begin Confirm the following before you download the installer: Your computer meets the Desktop system requirements /desktop/requirements . Tellann Desktop is published for 64 bit Windows only; macOS and Linux builds are not available. You have a Tellann account with access to at least one organization and application. See Create an application /get started/create an application if you do not have one. Git is installed and available on your `PATH` if you intend to attach a local repository. Browser only workflows do not use Git. Download and verify the installer Download the installer from the Tellann Desktop download page on tellann.co. Installer files follow the pattern `Tellann VERSION ARCH.exe`, for example `Tellann X.Y.Z x64.exe`. Before running it, verify the download /desktop/verify download by comparing the SHA 256 checksum of the file with the value published for that release. Do not run an installer whose checksum does not match. Run the installer 1. Open the downloaded `.exe` file. 2. Review the installation location. The installer is an assisted installer, so you can choose a different directory instead of accepting the default. 3. Complete the installer and start Tellann. Installation also registers the `tellann://` link scheme. Setup links that you open in a browser, such as a link to continue connecting a project, are handed to the installed application. If Tellann is already running, the link is passed to the open window instead of starting a second copy. Sign in Tellann Desktop authenticates through your system browser and then returns you to the application. After a successful sign in, the session is encrypted with Windows secure storage and saved in your user profile, so you stay signed in between launches. If Windows secure storage is unavailable, Desktop cannot keep the session; see Desktop troubleshooting /desktop/troubleshooting . Connect a project Select the application you want to work with, then choose how to connect it: Open a folder that already contains the project. Clone a repository into a location you choose. Attach a staging URL to observe a deployed environment. Start browser only without attaching any local files. Installing Desktop does not grant access to your files. Desktop begins with read only workspace analysis, and write access and command execution are requested separately when a workflow needs them. Production environments are observation only. Next steps Keep the application current with Desktop updates /desktop/updates . Add the SDK to your application with Install the SDK /get started/install the sdk . Record your first walkthrough with First demonstration /get started/first demonstration .

documents.title: Desktop System Requirements
documents.description: Operating system, architecture, network, and development-tool requirements for Tellann Desktop.
documents.body: Desktop System Requirements Check these requirements before installing Tellann Desktop. Requirements that only apply to a specific workflow, such as Git for repository features, name the workflow that needs them. Operating system | Requirement | Supported | | | | | Operating system | Windows 10 or later | | Architecture | 64 bit x64 | | macOS | Not available | | Linux | Not available | Tellann Desktop is built on Electron, which does not support Windows 7, Windows 8, or Windows 8.1. Install only an architecture that is listed for the release you download. Hardware Tellann has not published measured memory or disk minimums. Resource use grows with the size of the repository being analyzed and the number of browser sessions running at the same time, so large repositories and monorepos benefit from additional memory and free disk space. Network Desktop needs outbound HTTPS access to Tellann cloud services to sign in, synchronize approved results, and check for updates. Your system browser must also be able to reach the Tellann sign in page, because authentication happens in the browser. Proxies, VPNs, or firewalls that block or intercept HTTPS traffic can prevent sign in and synchronization. If your organization inspects TLS traffic, allow the Tellann domains used by your workspace. Development tools | Tool | Needed for | | | | | Git on `PATH` | Attaching, cloning, and checkpointing local repositories | | npm, pnpm, yarn, or bun | Detecting the project's package manager during workspace analysis | | A framework supported by the Tellann SDK | Instrumentation proposals | Desktop runs Git non interactively, so it never displays credential prompts. For private remotes, configure a credential helper such as Git Credential Manager before cloning from Desktop. Instrumentation proposals target the frameworks that the Tellann SDK supports. See Integration overview /integrations/integration overview for the current list. Permissions Installing the application does not give Tellann access to your repositories. Browser, read, write, and command permissions are separate, and each one is requested only when a workflow needs it. See Install Tellann Desktop /desktop/installation for the ways to connect a project.

documents.title: Verify a Desktop Download
documents.description: Confirm a Tellann Desktop installer's file name, checksum, and signature before you run it.
documents.body: Verify a Desktop Download Verify every Tellann Desktop installer before you run it. Verification confirms that the file on your computer is the file Tellann published for that release, and that it was not altered or replaced in transit. What to compare Each published release lists the metadata below alongside its installer. Compare all of it against the file you downloaded. | Field | What to check | | | | | File name | Matches `Tellann VERSION ARCH.exe` for the version and architecture you selected | | File size | Matches the published size | | SHA 256 checksum | Matches the published value exactly | | Signature | Matches the signing status stated for the release | Check the SHA 256 checksum Open PowerShell in the folder that contains the installer and run: ```powershell Get FileHash Algorithm SHA256 .\Tellann X.Y.Z x64.exe ``` Compare the `Hash` value in the output with the checksum published for the release. Every character must match. A checksum that only matches in its first or last characters is not a match. Check the signature In File Explorer, right click the installer, select Properties , and open the Digital Signatures tab. If the release states that the installer is signed, confirm that the tab lists Tellann as the signer and that Windows reports the signature as valid. If the release does not state that the installer is signed, the tab is absent and Windows SmartScreen may warn before the installer starts. Rely on the checksum in that case, and continue only when it matches. If verification fails Do not run the installer. Delete the file, download it again from the Tellann Desktop download page, and repeat the checks. If the mismatch persists after a fresh download, report it to Tellann support at https://tellann.co/contact. Include the file name, the checksum you computed, and where you downloaded the file from. See Desktop releases /desktop/releases for how published builds and withdrawn builds are handled.

documents.title: Desktop Updates
documents.description: How Tellann Desktop checks for and installs updates, which update channels exist, and why checks can be disabled.
documents.body: Desktop Updates Tellann Desktop can check an update feed for newer versions and install them. This page explains when checks run, what happens when an update is found, and why update checks can be disabled. How updates are applied When update checks are enabled, Desktop asks its configured update feed whether a newer version exists on its channel as the application starts. Finding an update does not download it. A newer version is not downloaded on its own when a check finds it. Installation happens on quit. A downloaded update is installed the next time you quit Tellann Desktop, so work in progress is not interrupted. Checks use HTTPS only. Desktop refuses an update feed address that does not use HTTPS. Update channels | Channel | Intended for | | | | | `stable` | General use. This is the default channel. | | `beta` | Teams that want early access to upcoming changes. | | `internal` | Pre release testing before a wider release. | See Desktop releases /desktop/releases for what each published release includes. When update checks are disabled | Reason | What it means | | | | | Development build | Checks never run in builds started from source code. Install a packaged release instead. | | No update feed configured | The build has no update feed address to check. | | Update feed is not HTTPS | The configured address does not use HTTPS, so it is ignored. | | Unknown channel | The configured channel is not `stable`, `beta`, or `internal`. | A disabled check does not affect the rest of the application. Desktop keeps running the installed version, and you can still update manually. Managed environments Organizations that host their own update feed configure it with environment variables on the machine that runs Desktop: `TELLANN UPDATE URL` sets the HTTPS address of the update feed. `TELLANN UPDATE CHANNEL` sets the channel to `stable`, `beta`, or `internal`. When it is not set, Desktop uses `stable`. Update manually You can install a newer version without the update feed. Download the installer from the Tellann Desktop download page, verify the download /desktop/verify download , and run it over the existing installation. If an update does not appear when you expect one, see Desktop troubleshooting /desktop/troubleshooting .

documents.title: Desktop Releases
documents.description: How Tellann Desktop versions, release entries, and withdrawn builds are published.
documents.body: Desktop Releases Every Tellann Desktop release is published with the metadata you need to choose the right build and verify it. This page explains how versions are numbered, what each release entry contains, and what happens when a build is withdrawn. Version numbers Versions use semantic versioning in the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: MAJOR changes alter existing workflows or compatibility. MINOR changes add capabilities without breaking existing workflows. PATCH changes contain fixes and small improvements. The version is part of the installer file name, for example `Tellann X.Y.Z x64.exe`. documents.body: Desktop Troubleshooting Use this page to resolve common problems with installing, signing in to, and running Tellann Desktop. Each section starts with the symptom you see. Windows blocks the installer If Windows SmartScreen shows a "Windows protected your PC" message, verify the download /desktop/verify download before doing anything else. Continue only when the SHA 256 checksum matches the value published for the release. If the checksum does not match, delete the file and download it again. A setup link does not open Desktop Links that start with `tellann://` are handled by the installed application. Confirm that Desktop was installed from a release installer. Builds started from source code do not register the link scheme. Allow your browser to open the Tellann application when it asks for permission. Reinstall Desktop to repair the link registration. Setup links are short lived. If a link has expired, start the connection again from the Tellann web application to get a new one. You are signed out every time Desktop starts Desktop stores your session with Windows secure storage. When secure storage is unavailable for your Windows account, for example in some virtual desktop or temporary profile configurations, Desktop cannot save the session and you must sign in on every launch. Use a standard, persistent Windows user profile to keep the session. Repository features fail Git is not found. Install Git for Windows, confirm that `git version` works in a new terminal, then restart Desktop so it picks up the updated `PATH`. Cloning a private repository fails. Desktop runs Git without interactive prompts, so it cannot ask for a username or password. Configure a credential helper such as Git Credential Manager and confirm that `git clone` works from a terminal first. A Git operation times out. Individual Git commands stop after 30 seconds. For a very large repository, clone or fetch it from a terminal, then open the folder in Desktop. No updates are offered Check the conditions in Desktop updates /desktop/updates when update checks are disabled . Builds started from source code never check for updates, and an update feed that is not HTTPS is ignored. You can always install a newer release manually. Sign in or synchronization fails with a network error Desktop needs outbound HTTPS access to Tellann services. Check that a proxy, VPN, or firewall is not blocking or intercepting the connection, and that your system browser can open the Tellann sign in page. See the network section of Desktop system requirements /desktop/requirements network . Contact support If a problem persists, contact Tellann support at https://tellann.co/contact. Include the Desktop version from the installer file name, your Windows version, and the steps that led to the problem. Never include access tokens, passwords, or repository secrets in a support request.

documents.title: Guided demonstrations
documents.description: Use a defined workflow to capture repeatable behavioral evidence.
documents.body: Guided demonstrations Use a defined workflow to capture repeatable behavioral evidence. Overview Guided demonstrations capture a scenario whose start, intended actions, and completion condition are already known. Tellann records the resulting events in one scoped session, derives states and transitions from that evidence, and associates the run with the workflow label you provide. Unlike a screen recording, the result is structured telemetry. Reviewers can inspect event order, API activity, errors, graph changes, and coverage without relying on pixels or video playback. When to use guided mode Choose a guided demonstration when the team has a specific journey to verify end to end, such as registration, sign in, checkout, password recovery, or a known failure and recovery path. It is especially useful when the same workflow must be compared across builds or environments. Use Exploratory mode when the route is intentionally open ended. Use Validation mode when an existing workflow and its expected boundaries are already established and the goal is to check new evidence against them. Before you begin Confirm that the application is connected, the intended non production environment is selected, and a minimal test event appears in Tellann. Write down the initial state, completion state, expected alternative or failure branches, and the evidence that will count as success. Apply privacy rules before opening screens that can contain credentials, personal information, payment details, or customer content. A demonstration inherits the collection behavior of the installed SDK; it does not override masking or retention policy. Run a guided demonstration 1. Open the application and environment that own the workflow. 2. Start a new demonstration and choose Guided . 3. Add a concise workflow label that describes the business outcome, not the tester or build number. 4. Begin from the documented initial state and perform only the actions required by the scenario. 5. Include the intended terminal state. If the scenario covers a failure, continue through the recovery outcome instead of stopping at the error. 6. Stop the demonstration and wait for processing to complete before opening its graph or coverage result. !TIP Keep the walkthrough focused. Unrelated navigation can create extra states and transitions that make comparison less useful. Review the results Open the session timeline first. Verify the environment, workflow label, start and end times, event order, and any API or error activity. Then inspect the derived graph and confirm that its states and transitions can be traced back to those events. Coverage reports show which known behavior was observed in this run. They do not prove the workflow is correct or complete. Treat an unexpected path as a prompt to inspect evidence, not as an automatic defect classification. Common errors No events received: verify the ingestion key, environment, SDK diagnostics, and collector reachability. Processing does not finish: preserve the demonstration and request identifiers, then check service health before retrying. States or transitions are missing: inspect the timeline for absent or out of order source events. Too many unrelated states: repeat the run from a clean initial state and avoid actions outside the labeled workflow. Sensitive values are visible: stop using the capture, correct privacy rules, rotate any exposed credential, and follow the data deletion procedure. Next steps Use Demonstration results /demonstration/results to interpret generated artifacts, Best practices /demonstration/best practices to improve repeatability, and Coverage comparison /coverage quality/coverage comparison when comparing evidence across runs. For a failure that cannot be explained from the graph, continue with Investigating failures /sessions replay/investigating failures .

documents.body: Event Model Learn how event model works within Events & Telemetry and how to apply it safely in Tellann. Overview Event Model is part of the canonical event contract, delivery behavior, validation rules, and privacy controls. It gives teams a shared way to describe what the application actually did and which evidence supports a quality conclusion. Mental model Read this topic in the sequence Connect → Observe → Demonstrate → Model → Analyze → Investigate → Act. The same event can contribute to a session, a state transition, a workflow, a graph edge, coverage, and a report without those artifacts becoming interchangeable. How to use it Choose the application and environment first, then narrow the evidence by workflow, session, time, endpoint, or event type. Use labels and metadata to make the captured behavior explainable to someone who did not run the original scenario. Interpretation Interpret the result together with its source events and collection conditions. Observed means Tellann received evidence for the behavior; it does not independently prove that the behavior is correct, secure, accessible, or complete. Limitations and responsibilities Customers remain responsible for instrumentation scope, lawful data collection, credential handling, privacy rules, and decisions made from the evidence. Tellann masks and isolates data according to configuration, but cannot infer every domain specific sensitive field. documents.body: Overview A practical overview of api reference in Tellann. Contract This reference describes the Overview surface as exposed through Tellann's API gateway. Canonical paths are derived from implemented gateway and service routes; roadmap only operations remain labeled Planned rather than shown as live calls. Authentication and scope Use the authentication mechanism required by the endpoint family and the narrowest applicable organization, application, and environment scope. Ingestion keys and user access tokens are not interchangeable. Request Encode every path value, validate required query parameters, and send JSON only when the operation accepts a body. Preserve the request ID returned by the gateway for investigation and support. Response Successful responses use the endpoint's documented status and JSON representation. Collection responses should be interpreted with their pagination metadata rather than assuming a complete dataset from one page. Errors and rate limits Handle validation, authentication, authorization, not found, conflict, rate limit, and service errors explicitly. Back off after a rate limit response and do not automatically repeat a non idempotent mutation without confirming its outcome. Interactive use Static request and response examples remain useful without credentials. The interactive console keeps its masked credential in component memory, sends only to the configured gateway origin, and requires confirmation for mutations.

Use a non production environment for initial verification whenever the task can affect telemetry or access. Procedure Follow the task in order and preserve the boundary between public application configuration and secret material. Make one scoped change, record its visible result, then continue to the next step. Verify the result Verify the nearest authoritative signal: SDK diagnostics for capture, an accepted event for ingestion, a session timeline for correlation, a graph or report for processing, and an audit record for administrative mutations. Correct the earliest failing boundary before repeating downstream actions. documents.body: Architecture Overview Learn how architecture overview works within Platform Architecture and how to apply it safely in Tellann. Overview Architecture Overview is part of the public system model from capture through ingestion, processing, storage, and presentation. It gives teams a shared way to describe what the application actually did and which evidence supports a quality conclusion. Mental model Read this topic in the sequence Connect → Observe → Demonstrate → Model → Analyze → Investigate → Act. The same event can contribute to a session, a state transition, a workflow, a graph edge, coverage, and a report without those artifacts becoming interchangeable. How to use it Choose the application and environment first, then narrow the evidence by workflow, session, time, endpoint, or event type. Use labels and metadata to make the captured behavior explainable to someone who did not run the original scenario. Interpretation Interpret the result together with its source events and collection conditions. Observed means Tellann received evidence for the behavior; it does not independently prove that the behavior is correct, secure, accessible, or complete. Limitations and responsibilities Customers remain responsible for instrumentation scope, lawful data collection, credential handling, privacy rules, and decisions made from the evidence. Tellann masks and isolates data according to configuration, but cannot infer every domain specific sensitive field.
